topics.topic: Definition and scope of runtime-loaded code from outside a release
questions: What counts as “code”, “loads”, and “outside the release” for this refusal—for example native shared libraries supplied by the host, executable helpers, plugins, generated modules, dynamically downloaded modules, or configuration interpreted by a dependency?

What exactly counts as “code”, “loads”, and “outside its release”, and does the prohibition cover plugins, modules from mounted paths, downloaded executable content, subprocess binaries, generated code, and code whose digest is checked only when loaded?
What counts as “code”, “loads”, and “outside its release” for deciding whether a dependency is prohibited?

quotes:
4. Registry has no dependency that loads code at run time from outside its

6. A release with a dependency that loads code at run time from outside
   the release is not made (rule 4).
judgement.divergence: One release process rejects a pinned dependency that downloads and executes an extension, while another admits the same release because it classifies only the pinned package as code; the release operator and the triggering caller observe whether the extension runs.
judgement.why: State 2 requires a refusal but leaves the terms that determine that refusal undefined, allowing admission of executable content that the prohibition may require the release process to reject.
options: Forbid every executable instruction, module, library, helper, plugin, or generated executable content obtained from outside the fixed release and base image.
Allow externally stored code when the release fixes and verifies its identity and digest before loading it.
Limit the prohibition to network-fetched or language-level plugin and module loading, while permitting documented host libraries, subprocess helpers, and interpreted configuration.
consequences: A broad definition maximizes reproducibility but may classify host libraries and executable helpers as release contents.
Digest-verified external code weakens the literal outside-the-release prohibition and requires a defined loading-time verification boundary.
A narrow definition permits executable behavior not enumerated among the release artifacts.
judgement.requirement:
4. Registry has no dependency that loads code at run time from outside its
   release.

judgement.why: State 2 fixes the refusal and no-start outcome, while identifying the actual kernel, covering alternate start paths, and choosing the enforcing installation or deployment boundary are deployment mechanisms.

judgement.owner_question: Which Linux documentation baseline or exact observable semantics define whether a kernel and filesystem are supported for no-follow opening, exclusive binding, rename, and flush?
options: Support every Linux kernel and filesystem conditionally on explicitly stated no-follow, exclusive-bind, rename, and flush semantics.
Name a minimum Linux API baseline and supported filesystem families.
Keep Linux versions unrestricted but enumerate the observable semantics an environment must provide, leaving deployment to qualify them.
consequences: An explicit semantic contract gives a stable support boundary but requires defining durability and atomicity precisely.
